EMS performance was found to be governed by load profile characteristics. The variability of the load profile is identified as the dominant predictor. All EMS exhibit worse sizing performance with increasing variability. Different dispatch strategies yield similar system sizing, indicating low sensitivity of sizing to dispatch details. Optimized EMS parameters show strong clustering, indicating robustness and enabling the derivation of heuristics for EMS parameter selection.​ The results imply that EMS tuning and system sizing can be decoupled with limited performance loss. This enables a separation of the HESS design process into sizing and EMS design, improving transparency, explainability, and modularity. Deadzone-based EMS provide strong baseline performance and constitute a benchmark for future EMS development.

title: Offshore hydrogen storage and transport enabled by clathrates: A techno-economic analysis
abstract: Hydrate-based hydrogen (H 2 ) storage technology (HyH2) offers notable advantages in the H 2 storage and transportation for wind-to-H 2 scenarios. However, the economic viability of HyH2 based on thermodynamic promoter solutions (TPS-HyH2) remains constrained by its slow formation kinetics. We proposed an innovative HyH2 utilizing nanoemulsion (NE-HyH2) which yields ultra-rapid kinetics within a 3-min cycle. In this study, we further conduct a techno-economic analysis of TPS-HyH2 and NE-HyH2 within a South China Sea wind farm scenario. Through a comprehensive evaluation of capital and operating costs, we observed a reduction in the levelized cost of H 2 storage and transportation (LCOHST) from $1.82/kg to $1.09/kg. The effect of key operating parameters, H 2 feed rate and transportation distance were analyzed, and the sensitivity analysis reveals that NE-HyH2 remains profitable operation distance up to 1350.0 km. Furthermore, the LCOHST and global warming potential (GWP) for NE-HyH2 and TPS-HyH2 were benchmarked with other H 2 storage technologies, revealing that NE-HyH2 demonstrates economic superiority for transport distance up to 3196.5 km and a low-carbon emission feature with GWP of 0.38 kg CO 2 eq./kg H 2 . Our findings suggest that NE-HyH2 is a cost-competitive and low-carbon maritime storage and transport method for offshore wind-to-H 2 systems within regional transport distances.

title: Toward modeling principles for space energy system optimization
abstract: With the aim of establishing modeling principles for space energy system optimization, this paper systematically reviews existing energy system modeling studies and assesses their transferability to extraterrestrial environments. Core concepts from terrestrial energy system modeling, including technology selection, capacity expansion, sector coupling, and storage optimization, provide a valuable foundation. However, space applications require adaptations to account for material and commodity flows, thermodynamic constraints, demand structures and mission criticality, and substantial uncertainty in technology performance, resource availability, and environmental conditions. These challenges highlight the need for stronger coupling between technology-level thermodynamic analyses and system-level optimization, explicit representation of mission-critical demands, and stochastic and other uncertainty-aware optimization approaches. Based on these findings, preliminary modeling principles and key directions for future methodological development are identified. To demonstrate their applicability, a lunar space village case study is developed for a sustained settlement over a one-year operational period. The optimized system combines nuclear power, solar photovoltaics, batteries, electrolyzers, and fuel cells, resulting in a levelized cost of electricity of approximately 7,800 EUR /MWh. This provides a first quantitative benchmark for future lunar energy infrastructures. Overall, the study provides a methodological foundation for space energy system optimization and supports the development of scientific knowledge and modeling capabilities for the expanding commercial, industrial, and energy-related activities in space.

title: Determining priorities for hydrogen infrastructure projects in Europe based on total system costs
abstract: Hydrogen production can provide important flexibility in a carbon-neutral European energy system, but its value depends on where and how pipeline and storage infrastructure are deployed. This study assesses the system benefits of hydrogen flexibility using REMix-Eur, a linear optimisation model of the European energy system with hourly resolution, 57 model regions and a technological scope of more than 100 technologies. We optimise a carbon-neutral 2050 target system and compare it with 24 scenarios in which hydrogen transfer and storage capacities are restricted relative to the cost-minimal case. The evaluation takes total system costs, investments, levelised cost of hydrogen, electrolyser operation, and regional infrastructure priorities for hydrogen technologies into account. Our results show that for the chosen scenario setup an inflexible hydrogen system increases annual system costs by 36 billion € or about 10 % compared to the cost-optimal case. Most of this penalty comes from restricting network rather than storage expansion. In the optimal case, Europe builds around 120 TWh of hydrogen cavern storage, with 57 % of it repurposed from previous natural gas utilisation. Electrolyser capacity ranges from around 330 GW to more than 500 GW across scenarios, and infrastructure enabling flexibility reduces the model-implied levelised cost of hydrogen from 64 € /MWh in the inflexible case to 51 € /MWh for the optimum. Our findings suggest that early hydrogen planning should prioritise cross-border pipeline corridors and the retrofitting of existing storage sites, especially in the North Sea region.

title: Waste-derived calcium chloride hexahydrate phase-change hydrogel composite for energy-efficient building thermal regulation
abstract: Decarbonising building energy use requires thermal energy storage materials that can reduce heating and cooling demand while remaining economically viable and resource efficient. Herein, a waste-derived calcium chloride hexahydrate phase-change hydrogel was developed for building envelope applications using recovered calcium chloride as the primary raw material. Bentonite, strontium chloride hexahydrate, and a three-dimensional polyacrylamide network were incorporated to improve nucleation, structural stability, and leakage resistance. The phase-change hydrogel was also characterised for its thermophysical properties and cycling stability, and its building-envelope performance was evaluated through thermal tests and energy assessment. The developed material exhibited a very low supercooling degree of 0.3 °C and a high latent heat of 173.2 J/g while showing good cycling stability by retaining over 86% of its latent heat with no observable phase separation after 600 cycles. When incorporated into building envelopes, a 20 mm layer reduced the average peak indoor temperature by 5.6 °C. Upon testing on 175 representative locations in China, the annual heating and cooling electricity saving ratio reached 3.0–17.5% in hot-summer–warm-winter zones. Furthermore, the developed material also exhibited a substantial cost advantage, with an estimated unit cost 38.6–90.3% lower than that of commercial alternatives. These results demonstrate that the waste-derived hydrogel offers a practical and economically viable approach to building thermal energy storage, with particularly strong potential in cooling-dominated regions.

title: Scenario space exploration for robust energy planning
abstract: Abstract Energy and climate assessments often contrast a few narrative scenarios, limiting insight into interacting uncertainties. We map a scenario space for a whole energy system model using more than 4,500 cost optimal runs, then analyse the ensemble with global sensitivity analysis, scatter plot diagnostics and scenario discovery. This workflow identifies influential drivers, reveals thresholds and regime switching, and distinguishes robust from contingent technology portfolios under demand and weather variability. It also answers the reverse policy question, which combinations of assumptions are sufficient to reach, or avoid, target outcomes. By shifting emphasis from point comparisons to distributions, interactions and condition sets, the approach supports interactive exploration of trade-offs and risks, and prioritises where higher fidelity follow up analysis is most valuable. Compared with conventional scenario studies, scenario space substantially increases robustness and exposes boundary conditions that are typically hidden by narrative comparisons, turning energy models into stress tests that delineate where policy performs reliably, and where it becomes brittle.

title: Two decades of vehicle-to-grid research show widely divergent profitability estimates
abstract: The global electric vehicle fleet already stores more energy than all dedicated grid-scale batteries combined, yet this capacity remains largely untapped as a storage resource for the energy transition. Vehicle-to-grid (V2G) can mobilize this capacity, but only if profits motivate vehicle owners to participate. After two decades of modeling research, reported annual profits still range from net losses to several thousand EUR per vehicle, without convergence over time. To explain this spread, we harmonize 589 reported outcomes from 78 studies to a common metric of EUR per vehicle per year and classify each study along three dimensions: the market segment in which V2G earns revenue, the market integration model that links EVs to that market, and the modeling assumptions used to derive each profit. While 86% of reported profits are positive (median 385 EUR), they span more than one order of magnitude. Two patterns emerge. Within studies, profitability behaves as economic reasoning predicts: it rises with deployable flexibility and falls with cycling costs. Across studies, this systematic response disappears because design choices such as cost scope, market environment, vehicle availability, and scheduling method vary simultaneously and cannot be disentangled. The disagreement therefore reflects study design, not V2G economics. Cost and regulatory conditions are now evolving favorably: battery prices are falling, real-world degradation costs are proving lower than the literature assumed, and regulatory frameworks are beginning to recognize bidirectional storage. The question is therefore no longer whether V2G can be profitable, but under which market and regulatory conditions it scales.

title: Simulation of Industrial Electrical Load Shapes (SIELS)
abstract: The industrial sector in the US consumes over 20% of the total electricity generated and growth in the sector could further increase its electricity demand and operational expenses. A well-resolved dataset of representative load profiles for industrial subsectors could provide a better understanding of their consumption patterns to stakeholders, and uncover opportunities to reduce these expenses for industrial customers. Therefore, in this study, we present Simulation of Industrial Electrical Load Shapes (SIELS), an empirical model that was developed to characterize hourly load profiles of seven energy-intensive industrial subsectors across the contiguous United States for the year 2018. Specifically, we analyzed the meter data from industrial customers in California to identify the most commonly occurring temporal patterns. We then developed a methodology to sample daily load shapes from this dataset and pair it with outputs from spatial datasets including the IGATE-E tool to develop hourly load profiles for industrial electricity demand. This marks the beginning of efforts to understand the heterogeneity of industrial loads and their operations. The results from the simulation are characterized using two metrics to analyze their hourly variability. In order to demonstrate a use case for this dataset, we explored the value of industrial load flexibility using broad-based assumptions for load shed. Our results indicate that industrial load flexibility could provide a significant amount of savings in capacity and billions of dollars in system costs.

title: Dry battery electrode processing: Advances, challenges, and future outlook
abstract: The growing demand for sustainable, high-performance energy storage is accelerating the transition toward cleaner and more efficient battery manufacturing technologies. Dry battery electrode (DBE) processing is emerging as a key enabler of this shift, as it eliminates toxic solvents, energy-intensive drying, and the large-scale recovery systems required in conventional wet electrode production. In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of DBE from the perspectives of processing technology, materials chemistry, sustainability, and application potential. Established and emerging DBE routes are summarized including binder fibrillation-based coating, powder-film formation, hot pressing, roll-to-roll lamination, and additive manufacturing. Furthermore, the influence of binder choice, powder interactions and microstructural design, on electrode integrity and electrochemical performance is investigated. The review also highlights the sustainability advantages of solvent-free manufacturing and outlines how DBE can support next-generation battery concepts, including solid-state systems. Additional dry-processible components, such as separators, membranes, and current collectors, are examined to illustrate broader opportunities for solvent-free cell fabrication. Finally, current challenges in scale-up, process control, and interface engineering are discussed, and strategies that may accelerate industrial implementation are presented. Together, these insights position DBE as a promising pathway toward more efficient, flexible, and environmentally friendly battery production.

title: SolarEV Cities for deep urban decarbonization: A critical review of integration gaps and transition pathways
abstract: Urban decarbonization is essential for meeting global climate goals; however, progress toward integrated low-carbon urban energy systems remains inadequately slow. The SolarEV City Concept integrates rooftop photovoltaic (PV) generation with electric vehicles (EVs) as city-scale distributed mobile energy storage, using EV batteries to increase the value and flexibility of urban rooftop PV. Modeling studies suggest that high-penetration PV+EV systems could supply 60–95% of municipal electricity demand under scenarios aligned with future sustainable-city development, but real-world integration remains limited. Despite rapid worldwide growth of both PV and EV markets, bidirectional Vehicle-to-Home/Building (V2H/V2B) and Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) applications have advanced unevenly, revealing a persistent PV-EV integration gap. This critical integrative review analyzes this gap using a socio-techno-economic framework encompassing six interdependent dimensions: climate, urban structure, technology, economics, policy, and society, across nine countries: Australia, China, France, India, Indonesia, Japan, the Netherlands, South Korea, and the United States. Cross-national comparison shows that implementation is constrained by fragmented bidirectional-charging standards, immature value-stacking and compensation models, distribution-grid and market-access constraints, regulatory separation between energy and transport sectors, and equity barriers that disproportionately limit access for renters, apartment residents, and lower-income households. Five transition-pathway archetypes, ranging from Japan’s resilience-driven V2H pathway to regulation-enabled commercial V2G pathways in France and the Netherlands, demonstrate that SolarEV Cities require a transition from parallel PV and EV promotion toward shared urban-energy visions, interoperable digital infrastructure, feeder-aware planning, inclusive market designs, and multi-stakeholder implementation platforms that convert rapid PV and EV innovation into scalable, resilient, and socially inclusive urban decarbonization.

title: Timing and feasibility windows for industrial heat electrification in the United States
abstract: Electrification is widely seen as central to industrial decarbonization, yet its climate value depends on both economic feasibility and the timing of adoption relative to changing grid emissions. Here we develop an integrated framework linking unit-level techno-economic assessment, policy stacking, marginal-emissions trajectories and capital turnover to evaluate U.S. industrial boiler electrification through 2050. We show that electrification is constrained by distinct policy feasibility windows, with strong heterogeneity across utilization levels and incumbent-asset conditions, and that single policy instruments are often insufficient to achieve cost parity. Conditional on adoption, climate outcomes depend on the alignment between industrial replacement cycles and regional declines in marginal grid emissions. Accelerated turnover and coordinated policy support can expand near-term feasibility, but premature deployment in emissions-intensive grids may delay mitigation gains. These results show that industrial electrification requires co-optimization of policy feasibility and decarbonization timing to target both cost-effective adoption and timely emissions reductions.

title: Who adopts where and when? Electric vehicle diffusion with building-level localization in Germany
abstract: The electrification of private vehicles is a central element of decarbonizing transport and energy systems. Accurately anticipating when and where electric vehicles will be adopted is critical for charging infrastructure planning, distribution grid planning, and energy system operation, yet most diffusion models represent adoption at aggregated spatial scales. Here we introduce an open, scalable, high-resolution technology diffusion framework that links household-level electric vehicle adoption with georeferenced building-level residential locations. The framework combines a synthetic population, household-to-building matching, car ownership modeling, and a national Bass diffusion trajectory to translate aggregate electric vehicle growth into localized adoption pathways. We apply the framework to Germany from 2025 to 2050 and evaluate its main components using Census marginals, household-to-building consistency metrics, and registered vehicle counts, demonstrating its suitability for spatially explicit electric vehicle diffusion analysis. The results reveal substantial spatial heterogeneity in electric vehicle diffusion across regions, municipalities, grid cells, and buildings. Differences in household income and the share of single-family houses shape local adoption trajectories, leading to higher adoption in West Germany than in East Germany and slightly higher adoption in rural than urban municipalities in aggregate. The framework provides an open and transferable basis for spatially explicit modeling of household technology diffusion. Future research can build on these findings by applying the framework to other technologies or by linking electric vehicle diffusion at georeferenced building-level locations to charging demand, system operation, and infrastructure planning.

title: User-redirection-aware co-optimization of public charging with local photovoltaics and battery storage
abstract: Rapid transport electrification creates spatially concentrated and temporally varying charging demand, making public charging infrastructure a joint investment and localized energy management problem. This study develops a co-optimization approach, from a charging point operator perspective, integrating incentivized user redirection as a flexibility measure into the spatial joint deployment of multi-class public chargers and on-site solar photovoltaic generation, and battery energy storage, together with retail tariff-responsive grid procurement and battery operations. Logic-based Benders decomposition is used to separate infrastructure decisions from the discrete annual operational problem under user redirection, dynamic time-of-use tariffs, land use constraints, seasonal solar variability, and spatiotemporal charging demand. The method is tested in a case study in Gothenburg, Sweden, using multiple spatial, transport, and energy data sources. Relative to the chargers-only case without user redirection, the combined photovoltaic, battery storage, and user redirection case increases annual net profit by SEK 19.10 million (3.94%), reduces grid purchases by 32.75 GWh/year (28.4%), while serving all charging demand. Within the photovoltaic and storage configuration, user-redirection increases profit by SEK 1.73 million (0.34%), reduces the public charger count by 14.8%, and reallocates 2.07 GWh/year (2.09%) of public demand. The results indicate that local photovoltaics and battery storage account for most of the reduction in grid electricity use, while incentivized user redirection reduces the required chargers and improves the operational use of local energy and charging capacity, consequently amplifying the benefits of PV with battery storage.

title: Coordinated market mechanism design and analysis for the integrated electricity, carbon emissions trading, green certificate, and hydrogen markets
abstract: As renewable penetration increases, the interdependencies among electricity, carbon-emissions trading, green-certificate, and hydrogen markets (ECGHM) become increasingly important, and MOlated single-market modeling is insufficient for designing cross-market coordination mechanisms. To address this issue, this paper develops a coordinated mechanism for integrated ECGHM, in which electricity trading, carbon-allowance compliance, green-certificate obligations, and hydrogen production decisions are jointly modeled within a unified framework. On this basis, the paper introduces three economically interpretable benchmark mechanisms within the same integrated market framework and examines their corresponding market outcomes through equilibrium analysis. Building on this theoretical benchmark, the paper further introduces hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning to simulate market outcomes under the coordinated mechanism in a multi-agent, multi-market, and multi-timescale setting, and to support mechanism-parameter sensitivity analysis and optimization. The case-study results show that the coordinated mechanism increases aggregate participant profit while maintaining social welfare close to the social-welfare-maximization benchmark.

title: Mind the temperature gap: Pit thermal energy storage in sector-coupled energy systems with high-temperature district heating
abstract: Pit thermal energy storage (PTES) provides large-scale thermal storage capacity in district heating systems, supporting flexibility on daily to seasonal scales. Most existing large-scale energy system studies on PTES ignore temperature differences between storage and the network, even though they reduce usable storage capacity and require temperature boosting during discharge. We quantify how temperature constraints shape the system-level value of PTES using PyPSA-DE, a sector-coupled capacity expansion model of Germany, in a net-zero emission scenario for 2045. The model explicitly resolves Germany’s 40 largest district heating systems with multiple heat sources—including geothermal, river and sea water as well as electrolyzer waste heat pumps. We compare counterfactual systems without PTES, idealized systems with PTES but without temperature constraints, and temperature-aware systems in which discharge is boosted by resistive heaters or heat pumps. PTES reduces total annual system costs by 133–844 M€ a −1 across the temperature-aware scenarios relative to tank storage only. Lowering network temperatures increases these PTES benefits to roughly 3 times their high-temperature level, and combining PTES with lower network temperatures reduces district-heating costs by up to 13%. Idealized scenarios without temperature constraints can raise estimated total system savings to more than 4 times the values obtained in the temperature-aware cases. PTES provides economic value even under current high temperatures, but its contribution remains limited during peak-demand periods when boosted discharge becomes uneconomic. The findings highlight PTES’ role in leveraging low-price electricity through electrified heating and the importance of explicitly accounting for temperature constraints in energy system models.

title: Integrating water electrolysis, wastewater treatment and district heating: Geospatial suitability and techno-economic potential in Europe
abstract: This study assesses the Europe-wide potential for multi-sector integration of water electroly-sis, wastewater treatment plants, and district heating networks, enabling by-product oxygen and waste heat utilization to improve energy efficiency and reduce system costs. Wastewater treatment plants (WWTP) can serve as geographically fixed anchor points for such integra-tion, requiring the consideration of land-use and infrastructure criteria to assess its feasibility. A hybrid methodology narrows the theoretical potential to geospatially and economically via-ble WWTP sites. First, a GIS-based analysis applying energy infrastructure access and land-use criteria (flood risks, protected zones, and space availability) identifies geospatially feasible WWTP sites. Second, an optimization model evaluates site-specific economic viability. Re-sults indicate that multi-sector integration is geospatially and economically viable at multiple European WWTP sites. Deployment is primarily limited by hydrogen pipeline infrastructure access, followed by nature reserves. These criteria reduce an initial set of 197 large-scale WWTPs of at least 500,000 population equivalents to 60 geospatially feasible WWTP sites (30.5%). Of these feasible sites, 35 offer strong district heating integration potential with con-nection distances below 5 km to existing district heating networks. Furthermore, by-product oxygen utilization achieves potential cost reductions between 0.05 and 0.20 EUR/kgH2. Nev-ertheless, overall hydrogen supply costs remain predominantly driven by renewable electricity potentials and financing conditions, with minimum costs achieved in Spain. Realizable poten-tial may be further limited by site-specific factors such as grid capacity, permitting, and land ownership, which are not captured at the European scale of this study.

title: Ship-shore energy systems for maritime electrification: Voyage-energy provision, configurations and resilience
abstract: Maritime decarbonisation requires a shift towards low- and zero-emission energy systems, while the viability of electrified vessels depends on how voyage energy is provided onboard and replenished externally. Existing reviews mainly organise the field around technologies, vessel configurations and replenishment solutions, with less attention to how energy provision and system constraints shift across the ship-shore system. We reviewed literature published primarily from 2000 to 2026 on onboard capability, external replenishment, ship-shore coordination and resilience, and synthesised these areas through the perspective of voyage-energy provision. The review identifies two energy-supply pathways. Shore-electric operation relies on sustained external electricity supply, while fuel-carried electric operation relies more on onboard fuel storage and conversion. Four representative configurations are distinguished as battery-dominant shore-electric, range-extended hybrid, power-buffered hybrid and fuel-dominant electric. Three illustrative case studies examine how replenishment conditions and onboard capability affect operational feasibility across representative vessel services. As reliance shifts from external supply towards onboard autonomy, the main constraints move from replenishment access and port-side supply capacity towards onboard energy storage and conversion capability. These dependencies also shape vulnerability to physical and cyber disruptions and the continuity of energy services. These findings can support early assessment of likely deployment constraints under different operating and infrastructure conditions and help coordinate vessel and shore-side energy planning.
